The title of this autobiography is a deliberate play on a foundational philosophical statement, replacing existence with action. The phrasing reflects a belief that identity, at least in this context, is defined through performance rather than being.
This aligns closely with the author’s playing style: calm, measured, and often seemingly detached from the intensity of the game, operating as the tempo-setter rather than the runner.
Recently, this composure has even been humorously reinterpreted as someone who appears too effortless to be “working” in the conventional sense on the pitch.

Beginning in at least the 15th century, this cross-shaped race game—whose name is derived from a Sanskrit word meaning “four”—was widely played across the Indian subcontinent. Archaeological evidence of the game exists in the form of boards carved directly into the stone floors of historic monuments, indicating both its portability and popularity.
It was notably a favourite pastime of a prominent Mughal emperor, who is said to have played it on a life-sized board with human participants. Over time, the game influenced the development of a simplified Western board game that remains popular today.
